notes.meaning: Elijah suddenly appears before King Ahab to announce that no dew or rain will fall for years until he gives the word. He declares that he stands in the presence of the living God, which directly challenges Baal, the Canaanite god whom Ahab worshipped as the lord of rain and storms. The severe drought was God's punishment on the nation for turning to idols, exactly as Moses had warned in the law.

The Lord speaks directly to Elijah right after his bold warning to the king. God does not leave His prophet alone after giving him a dangerous task, but immediately steps in with clear direction for his next step.

God tells Elijah to leave Samaria, travel eastward toward the Jordan River, and hide near the Brook of Cherith. This quiet hiding place kept him safe from Ahab's anger and prevented the king from begging him to bring the rain back before the punishment had done its work.

God promises that Elijah will have fresh water to drink from the stream and that wild ravens will bring him food. God often chooses simple or unexpected creatures to care for His people when ordinary human help is gone.
Elijah immediately obeys the Lord and goes to live in the lonely valley east of the Jordan. He shows total trust in God's care rather than seeking comfort or safety among people.

Every morning and evening, the ravens bring Elijah bread and meat while he drinks from the brook. Even though ravens are birds of prey that do not naturally share food or even care well for their own young, God directed them to feed His prophet every day.

After some time, the stream dries up because there has been no rain in the land. Elijah had to watch his own water supply vanish, which tested his faith to keep trusting the Lord even when earthly comforts failed.
The word of the Lord comes to Elijah again as soon as the brook runs dry. God never forgets His servants, and His new instructions arrive at the exact moment their old provisions run out.

The Lord directs Elijah to leave Israel and go to Zarephath, a town near Sidon in foreign Phoenician territory. God reveals that a poor widow living in the very home country of Baal worship will provide for him.

Elijah obeys God and travels to Zarephath, where he finds a widow gathering firewood at the town gate. He tests whether she is the woman chosen by God by asking her for a cup of water. Even though water was precious during a drought, she is willing to help a stranger right away.

As the woman goes to fetch the water, Elijah calls out and asks her to bring him a piece of bread as well. This asked for an even greater sacrifice, testing her kindness during a time of widespread famine.

The woman swears by the living Lord, Elijah's God, that she has no baked bread at all. She only has a handful of flour in a jar and a drop of cooking oil in a jug, and she is gathering sticks to cook one final meal before she and her son starve. Her answer shows her extreme poverty, yet also shows she recognized Elijah as a true prophet of Israel's God.

Elijah tells the anxious mother not to be afraid, but asks her to bake a small loaf for him first before making food for herself and her son. This was a severe test of faith, asking a starving mother to put God's prophet ahead of her own child's need.

Elijah gives her God's promise that her jar of flour will not empty and her jug of oil will not run dry until rain returns to the land. God promises to replace the food she gives away with an endless supply through His divine power.

The widow believes the prophet's message, bakes the bread for Elijah first, and finds that food lasts for her whole family for a long time. Her willingness to trust God's promise when everything looked hopeless brought survival to her entire household.
Just as the Lord had promised through Elijah, the jar never ran out of flour and the jug never ran out of oil. Every time she went to prepare a meal, God miraculously renewed what was needed.

Sometime later, the widow's son becomes severely ill, grows worse, and completely stops breathing. Even though this family had experienced daily miracles of food, they were not shielded from sudden pain and grief.

Overcome with grief, the woman cries out to Elijah and asks if he came to bring God's attention to her past sins by taking her son's life. When sudden disaster strikes, people often feel guilty and assume God is punishing old wrongdoing, even when God intends to show His mercy through the trouble.

Elijah does not argue with the grieving mother, but gently takes the dead boy from her arms and carries him up to his own guest room. He lays the child on his bed, taking the family's deep sorrow straight into his private place of prayer.

Elijah pours out his heart to God, asking why the Lord would bring such heartbreak on the kind widow who had taken him into her home. He prays with great honesty, pleading with God to show mercy to this grieving mother.

Elijah stretches himself over the boy three times and earnestly asks the Lord to return the child's life to him. This action showed his deep love and served as an outward sign of God's life-giving power coming down upon the body. His prayer also shows that the human soul remains real and alive even when separated from the body.

The Lord answers Elijah's prayer, and the boy's life returns so that he revives. This is the very first resurrection from the dead recorded in Scripture, proving that Israel's God has total power over life and death.

Elijah carries the living child downstairs and gives him back to his mother, announcing that her son is alive. The sorrow of the home turns to great joy as God rewards the prophet's prayer and the mother's kindness.

The woman confesses with full certainty that Elijah is truly a man of God and that the Lord's message from his mouth is absolute truth. Through this miracle, a Gentile woman who once knew little about God came to have complete faith in the God of Israel.
